root.note: A reconstructed form, recorded later as Old High German blanch ‘shining, white’.

stages.when: already in the Cantar de Mio Cid

history: You would expect the Spanish word for white to be Latin. It isn't. Latin had albus, but Germanic blank, ‘shining, bright’, pushed it out; one account says it first described pale horses. Old English had blanca for a white horse too. By the time of the Cantar de Mio Cid, Spain's oldest great poem, blanco was already at home in Spanish. The Latin word didn't quite vanish. It lives on in alba, ‘dawn’, and albino. English blank and German blank are the same Germanic word, but they took the meaning ‘empty’ or ‘shiny’. A página en blanco, ‘blank page’, brings the two senses back together.
historyEinfach: Blanco means ‘white’. The word is not Latin. The Latin word was albus. Germanic peoples said blank, ‘bright, shining’. Maybe they used it for pale horses. Spanish took this word, and it pushed out the Latin word. Albus lives on in alba, ‘dawn’, and albino. English blank comes from the same word.

elsewhere.text: English blank is a relative of blanco, and Spanish en blanco ‘blank’ brings the two meanings together.
German blank now means shiny, not white: same word, different direction.
